Post em que boiadeira brincou com o cantor Leonardo — Foto: Redes Sociais

A cantora sul-mato-grossense Ana Castela brincou, neste domingo (27), sobre a mudança no visual do cantor Leonardo. Nas redes sociais, os dois trocaram comentários sobre o artista ter “desinchado” após um período de “detox” de álcool.

Natural de Sete Quedas , Ana Castela também tem adotado hábitos mais saudáveis, com atividade física diária e mudanças na alimentação.

Na postagem, o cantor goiano aparece tomando chá e diz que dará um recado no fim desta segunda-feira (28).

Nos comentários, Ana Castela escreveu: "vc tá desinchado", brincou. Em resposta, Leonardo disse: "e eu por acaso estava inchado Ana ? 🤔😂".

Em outros comentários, fãs voltaram a citar o antigo relacionamento entre Ana Castela e o filho de Leonardo. Um deles escreveu: "é de tanto chorar por vc ter deixado de ser nora dele".

Leonardo mudou de aparência ao adotar um novo estilo de vida, fazendo "detox" de álcool. — Foto: Redes Sociais

Nas redes socais, a artista compartilhou registros de um treino de costas na academia. Durante os exercícios, a artista mostrou a rotina de preparação física e chamou a atenção ao levantar 20 kg em atividades como remada e barra.

Ana aparece realizando os movimentos com pesos, acompanhada de orientações durante o treino. A cantora também exibiu parte da sequência de exercícios voltados ao fortalecimento da musculatura das costas.

articles.title: Cleusimar Cardoso: mãe de Djidja vai para o regime semiaberto | G1
articles.standfirst: Cleusimar foi condenada, em julho deste ano, a 10 anos e 11 meses de prisão por crimes relacionados ao tráfico de cetamina em Manaus. Segundo a sentença, ela era apontada como a principal articuladora e líder do grupo investigado no caso.
articles.summary: Condenada por tráfico de cetamina no Caso Djidja Cardoso, Cleusimar Cardoso cumprirá pena em regime semiaberto com uso obrigatório de tornozeleira eletrônica em Manaus.
articles.body:
Djidja Cardoso com a mãe Cleusimar Cardoso e o irmão Ademar Cardoso. — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

A mãe da ex-sinhazinha do Boi Garantido Djidja Cardoso, Cleusimar de Jesus Cardoso , vai deixar a prisão após a Justiça do Amazonas conceder a progressão do regime fechado para o semiaberto . A mudança passa a valer a partir desta segunda-feira (28). A decisão é da juíza Sabrina Cumba Ferreira, da 2ª Vara de Execução Penal de Manaus .

A mãe da ex-sinhazinha do Boi Garantido Djidja Cardoso, Cleusimar de Jesus Cardoso, vai deixar a prisão nesta segunda-feira (28) para cumprir o restante da pena no regime semiaberto. A progressão do regime fechado foi concedida pela Justiça do Amazonas. A decisão é da juíza Sabrina Cumba Ferreira, da 2ª Vara de Execução Penal de Manaus.

Com a mudança, Cleusimar deverá usar tornozeleira eletrônica e cumprir uma série de regras , como permanecer em casa durante a noite e nos fins de semana.

Cleusimar foi condenada, em julho deste ano , a 10 anos e 11 meses de prisão por crimes relacionados ao tráfico de cetamina em Manaus. Segundo a sentença, ela era apontada como a principal articuladora e líder do grupo investigado no caso.

A Justiça também reconheceu 12 dias de abatimento da pena por atividades realizadas por Cleusimar durante o período em que está presa.

Foram quatro dias pela leitura de um livro, sete pelos 21 dias trabalhados e um pela participação no Projeto Remicine. As atividades foram realizadas em agosto de 2026.

A decisão também registra que Cleusimar teve bom comportamento na prisão. Com isso, segundo a Justiça, ela cumpriu os requisitos necessários para a mudança de regime.

Com a progressão, Cleusimar deverá ser cadastrada no sistema Chronos e usar tornozeleira eletrônica.

Ela terá que permanecer em casa das 22h às 6h, de segunda a sexta-feira. Nesse período, poderá sair apenas para trabalhar, estudar ou fazer tratamento de saúde previamente informado à Central de Monitoramento.

Nos fins de semana, feriados e dias de folga, o recolhimento deverá ser integral na residência cadastrada.

Cleusimar também não poderá mudar de endereço ou deixar Manaus sem autorização da Justiça. Ela deverá ainda atender às convocações das autoridades.

A decisão proíbe o uso de armas, bebidas alcoólicas e drogas. Ela também não poderá cometer novos crimes.

Cleusimar foi condenada em 22 de julho de 2026, junto com outras seis pessoas , em uma nova sentença relacionada ao esquema investigado pela Operação Mandrágora.

Também foram condenados Ademar Farias Cardoso Neto, irmão de Djidja , José Máximo Silva de Oliveira, Hatus Moraes Silveira, Verônica da Costa Seixas, Sávio Soares Pereira e Bruno Roberto da Silva Lima.

As penas dos sete condenados variaram de oito anos e seis meses a 10 anos e 11 meses de prisão.

Segundo a sentença, o grupo utilizava a rede de salões de beleza Belle Femme e a seita religiosa "Pai, Mãe, Vida" para distribuir e aplicar cetamina . A substância é usada como anestésico veterinário e, segundo a investigação, era obtida de forma ilegal e utilizada em rituais do grupo.

Outros três réus — Emicley Araújo Freitas, Claudiele Santos da Silva e Marlisson Vasconcelos Dantas — foram absolvidos por falta de provas suficientes.

A condenação de julho foi uma nova decisão sobre o mesmo processo. A sentença anterior havia sido anulada pela Justiça 10 meses antes .

Depois da regularização das provas periciais, a Justiça entendeu que havia elementos suficientes para confirmar os crimes e a responsabilidade dos condenados.

Djidja Cardoso, empresária e ex-sinhazinha do Boi Garantido que morreu por suspeita de overdose — Foto: TV Globo/Reprodução

Djidja Cardoso foi encontrada morta em 28 de maio de 2024 , em Manaus. Ela ficou conhecida por interpretar a sinhazinha do Boi Garantido e foi uma das principais atrações do Festival de Parintins durante cinco anos.

Segundo o laudo preliminar citado na investigação, ela morreu após sofrer um edema cerebral, que comprometeu o funcionamento do coração e da respiração. O documento não apontou o que teria causado o edema.

A principal linha de investigação da polícia foi a possibilidade de uma overdose de cetamina.

Durante as investigações, policiais encontraram frascos da substância enterrados no quintal da casa de Djidja. Também foram apreendidas caixas de cetamina, seringas, frascos, bulas e cartelas de medicamentos.

articles.title: ‘It’s a tough life’: Katrina Kaif reveals how her mother left London and now lives in a Tamil Nadu village with limited electricity to help children in India
articles.summary: Katrina Kaif's mother, Suzanne Turquotte, has spent more than 15 years living and working in rural Tamil Nadu, far removed from the world of Bollywood.
articles.body: Katrina Kaif's mother, Suzanne Turquotte, has spent more than 15 years living and working in rural Tamil Nadu, far removed from the world of Bollywood. Suzanne moved from London to Tamil Nadu in 2008 and founded Relief Projects India (RPI), a grassroots organisation working with children and families in villages around Usilampatti in Madurai district. And this was told by Katrina herself. She has previously spoken about the conditions in which her mother lives, including limited electricity and unreliable internet connectivity. In an interview by ABP News, Katrina described her mother's life as difficult but said Suzanne continues to live there because she enjoys helping people. “It’s a tough life,” Katrina said while talking about her mother's life in the village.Katrina Kaif on her mother's life in a Tamil Nadu villageAs reported by ABP News, Katrina said her mother lives in a village in Tamil Nadu where basic conveniences are not always readily available. The actress explained that electricity can be unavailable for several hours, while internet connectivity can also be unreliable. These conditions can make even video calls difficult. Suzanne has lived in the village since moving to Tamil Nadu in 2008 and continues her work there. In 2014, while promoting her film Fitoor, the actor again opened up about her mother’s influence on her life. “My mother lives in Madurai and runs a school for blind children. Because of her charity work, I have achieved everything in life. All of this is because of the blessings she received,” Katrina had said.Suzanne moved from London to Tamil NaduSuzanne moved to Tamil Nadu in 2008 and established Relief Projects India. According to the organisation's official website, it is a grassroots nonprofit working with children and families in rural villages of Usilampatti Taluk, Madurai district. It was founded with a focus on giving children from disadvantaged backgrounds access to education. Its work initially grew around free evening tuition centres for children attending government schools. The programme expanded across villages in Usilampatti Taluk, with particular attention to girls' education and reducing school dropout. Over time, the organisation expanded beyond education. The organisation says it currently works across 25 villages and has reached more than 14,000 people.Suzanne also co-founded a schoolOne of the organisation's major projects is Mountain View School, which was established in 2015. According to the school's official website, it was founded to provide English-medium education to children from economically disadvantaged rural farming communities around Usilampatti. The school began as a nursery with fewer than 30 children between the ages of three and five. The enrollment rose from 54 students in 2016 to 305 students in 2025-26. The school currently runs from LKG to Grade 5. Susanna Turcotte is the school's co-founder, education adviser and a member of its advisory board.Katrina has spoken about the influence of her mother's workKatrina's comments about her mother provide a personal perspective on the life Suzanne has chosen. Rather than returning to an urban lifestyle, Suzanne has continued to live close to the communities where her organisation operates. articles.title: Data center developer offers $10,000 checks to 4,500 households if the 1,300-acre facility is approved
articles.summary: Data center developer proposes paying checks of $10,000 per household to sway public sentiment.
articles.body:
NorthPoint Development wants to build a data center on 1,300 acres in the Pocono foothills near Hazle Township, Pennsylvania, offering $10,000 per household as part of its charm offensive.

Despite the town's median income of $60,000, locals are widely against the data center development plans due to concerns about potential impacts on property values, noise pollution, and a distrust of AI moguls and local government representatives.

Hazle Township residents have received offer letters from NorthPoint since June, with some expressing that while the $10,000 would be handy, many are not eager to welcome the data center for the payout, feeling that the offer is insufficient and potentially insulting.

NorthPoint Development wants to build a data center on 1,300 acres in the Pocono foothills, near Hazle Township, Pennsylvania. As well as seeking to charm the local government with various funding packages, it has proposed paying checks of $10,000 per household. Despite the Pennsylvania town's median income of $60,000, the offer isn't being warmly welcomed by locals, reports the Wall Street Journal . Those interviewed were widely against the data center development plans and cited several reasons for being averse to accepting the payout. The major concerns regarded potential impacts on property values, the specter of noise pollution , and a distrust of both the AI moguls and local government representatives.

Offer letters began to be received by Hazle Township back in June. The WSJ recently talked to several residents about NorthPoint's $10,000 offer. While some say the $10,000 would be handy, it couldn't find many residents who were "eager to welcome the data center for the payout," in the journal's words. We'd point out that opinion polling can often be inaccurate, as what people say and what they do, voting-wise, doesn't always line up.

Interviewees cited a number of key reasons for their data center development aversion. We distilled the following points from the source:

Distrust of AI moguls and local authorities

Potential negative impact on property prices

Traditionally, developers have offered towns and cities packages worth tens of millions, including funding for local services . But direct cash payments to residents represent a new phase of their charm offensive, the WSJ indicates. Perhaps the idea for the direct payments to residents came after "a raucous public meeting last year, where angry locals asked what they had to gain by supporting the data center," ponders the source.

The locals won't just get the direct payout, though. Other funds up to $120 million over the next 15 years have been dangled like a carrot for community and local services investments — improved schools, emergency services, and so on.

Meanwhile, Hazle Township's government already rejected the data center project on zoning grounds last year, and it has enacted a temporary moratorium on data center construction. Finally, the $10,000 offer to households is simply not enough in many interviewed folks' opinions. Residents could feel insulted by it, regarding the offer as a bribe, concludes the WSJ report.

articles.title: North Carolina reused dredged material that would have been discarded offshore to rebuild an eroding bird island near Wanchese; within a week, oystercatchers and terns were exploring the new habitat
articles.summary: A North Carolina island that had been losing land to erosion has been restored using material removed while clearing a nearby navigation channel.
articles.body: A North Carolina island that had been losing land to erosion has been restored using material removed while clearing a nearby navigation channel. The dredged material, which would otherwise have been placed offshore, was used to rebuild Wells Island near Wanchese and create open, sandy habitat for nesting waterbirds. Within a week of the restoration work, wildlife officials found American Oystercatchers and a group of terns exploring the newly created habitat, according to North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission (NCWRC).The restoration was completed in March through a collaboration between the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), Gator Dredging and the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission (NCWRC). The work was linked to a dredging project near Wanchese that was needed to maintain a section of the Old House Channel.The project was designed to serve two purposes. It would help keep the navigation channel open while also giving material removed from the channel a useful purpose. Instead of simply placing the material offshore, officials used it to restore Wells Island, which had experienced considerable erosion in recent years.The restoration also comes as North Carolina's coastal bird nesting islands face continued erosion. A separate analysis by NCWRC examined 48 non-barrier coastal islands known to have been used by nesting wading birds. It found that 19 currently had no area of emergent habitat, while 10 had experienced 50% to 95% erosion. Another 19 islands had been eroded by up to 25%.Dredged material used to rebuild Wells IslandNCWRC owns and manages several islands along the North Carolina coast for the conservation of nesting waterbirds. Wells Island was one of those sites, but erosion had reduced its habitat over recent years.When the USACE planned maintenance work on the Old House Channel, officials looked for a beneficial use for the material that would be removed. NCWRC and USACE have worked together for decades on ways to keep waterways navigable while also supplying sand for beaches and islands, including sites protected for nesting waterbirds.Wells Island was identified as a suitable location for the material. Staff from USACE and NCWRC worked together to design an island that could meet the habitat needs of birds while also reducing erosion.The dredged material was piped from the navigation channel to Wells Island. Temporary berms were used to keep the material within the planned area while it accumulated. Bulldozers were then used to smooth and shape the deposited material.The result was an expanse of open, sandy habitat. According to NCWRC, this type of habitat is suitable for many species of nesting waterbirds.Birds explored the new habitat within a weekThe first signs of wildlife use came soon after the restoration work was finished. During a site visit the following week, NCWRC staff found a pair of American Oystercatchers and a group of terns exploring the newly created habitat.The observation came as officials continue to track the condition of coastal nesting islands across the state. NCWRC's analysis found that erosion and changing water levels are important threats to these areas and need to be monitored for species identified as being of conservation concern.The wider analysis looked at known non-barrier coastal islands used by nesting wading birds. Researchers used nesting records going back to 1975 and examined colour images from Google Earth dating back to 2003. They mapped the shoreline of each island for years when clear imagery was available.The findings showed substantial changes in several nesting islands. Of the 12 islands that had nesting wading birds in 2023, nine had experienced up to 25% erosion, while three had experienced between 50% and 95% erosion.One island used by Little Blue Herons and Snowy Egrets in the Albemarle and Currituck sounds had also changed considerably. It measured 4.5 acres in 2003 but had fallen to 1.9 acres by 2024.Restoration combines navigation and habitat needsThe Wells Island project shows how material removed during dredging can be used for habitat restoration. In this case, the same work needed to maintain a navigation channel also provided material that could be used to rebuild an eroding island.The restoration involved several stages. The dredged material was transported through pipes to the island, where temporary berms helped hold it in place. Heavy equipment then shaped the material into the planned habitat.NCWRC said partnerships of this kind are important as development continues along the coast and waterbirds need areas free from disturbance where they can nest.You use AI every day. articles.title: People jump from building windows to escape as Russian jet-powered drone hits Kyiv science academy - video
articles.summary: A Russian jet-powered drone struck Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv, prompting a rescue operation, Ukraine’s foreign ministry said.
articles.body: A Russian jet-powered drone struck Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv, prompting a rescue operation, Ukraine’s foreign ministry said. Videos circulating on social media appeared to show people jumping from the building’s windows as they tried to escape the strike.The incident came amid a wider wave of Russian attacks across Ukraine that killed three people and injured at least nine in Kyiv, according to Ukrainian officials. The extent of the damage to the academy building and the number of people affected were not immediately clear.The foreign ministry said the academy, one of Ukraine’s central scientific research institutions, had been hit in the heart of Kyiv. It called on UNESCO to support the country’s scientific community and strip Russia of its voice and voting rights within the organisation."The National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine is one of our country’s central institutions of scientific research, bringing together generations of Ukrainian researchers. Today, its building in the heart of Kyiv was hit by a Russian strike. A rescue operation is ongoing.Russia continues to strike civilian sites across Ukraine, damaging essential infrastructure.Every Russian strike must receive a strong response and increased pressure on the aggressor.We call on @UNESCO to stand with Ukraine's scientific community and strip Russia of its voice and voting rights within the organisation."Three killed in Russian attacks across UkraineRussian attacks killed three people in two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, while strikes on Kyiv injured nine people, including a child, local officials said.Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said six of the injured were being treated in hospital. A drone struck a high-rise apartment building in an eastern suburb, triggering a fire that was later extinguished by emergency crews.Drones also hit areas near a kindergarten and a playground in two districts, while debris from another drone caused a fire elsewhere in the city. No casualties were reported in those incidents.In the northern city of Sumy, three glide bombs struck near a family support centre, killing two people, regional governor Oleh Hryhorov said. In Kharkiv, a drone hit a car, killing the driver, prosecutors said.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the attacks, describing strikes on civilian targets as "terrorism"."Russia has no military objective whatsoever in doing this," Zelenskiy wrote in a post on X. "It is purely an attempt to break people and inflict as much harm as possible on our society."Zelenskyy said Russia had deployed 277 attack drones of various types since Saturday, including 155 jet-powered drones. He also said targets in Kyiv included a building used as a residence by the Saudi Arabian ambassador.Ukraine reports attacks on communications infrastructureUkraine’s largest mobile service provider told Interfax Ukraine that Russian forces had struck its headquarters amid continued attacks on the country’s data centres and communications infrastructure. There were no casualties, the company said.Russia’s defence ministry said its forces had struck two data centres, according to Reuters. The ministry did not provide further details in the material available.Why jet-powered drones are harder to interceptRussia’s use of jet-powered drones marks a further development in its long-range aerial attacks on Ukraine. Earlier models, including the propeller-driven Geran-1 and Geran-2, were slower and could be easier for air defences to intercept.A report published by The Conversation said Russia had introduced successive jet-powered variants, including the Geran-3 in 2025 and the Geran-4 later that year. The Geran-5 was first used operationally in August 2026, according to the report.The Geran-5 has a reported top speed of about 600 kilometres per hour, a range of up to 1,000 kilometres and an operating altitude of around 6,000 metres. Its speed, altitude and reported anti-jamming capabilities make it more difficult to intercept than earlier models, the report said.Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Colonel Yuriy Ihnat told the Financial Times on September 14 that Ukraine was intercepting about 60% of attacks by the Geran-5, compared with a 95% interception rate against other drone variants.The Conversation report also said Ukraine had been relying more heavily on fighter jets to shoot down the new drones. It cited Ukrainian military intelligence findings that components identified in the Geran-5 included a Chinese-supplied jet engine, US-made digital processors and German-manufactured transistors.The report said Russia was prioritising production of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 ahead of an autumn and winter campaign. Ukraine, meanwhile, has raised concerns over the availability of air defence missiles capable of intercepting the newer drones.The strike on Kyiv’s National Academy of Sciences comes amid a broader pattern of Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. The circumstances of the strike and the extent of damage to the academy building remain unclear.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Australian court rejects indigenous activist’s bid to prosecute King Charles over genocide; says ‘will take fight to ICC after exhausting domestic options’
articles.summary: An Australian court has denied Indigenous activist Uncle Robbie Thorpe's private prosecution against King Charles III over claims of genocide against Indigenous Australians, prompting a potential move to the International Criminal Court.
articles.body: An Australian appeals court has rejected an Indigenous activist’s attempt to bring a private prosecution against King Charles III over allegations that Australia’s treatment of Indigenous people amounts to genocide.Three judges at Victoria state’s Court of Appeal ruled against 68-year-old Uncle Robbie Thorpe on Monday, marking his third legal defeat since he began pursuing the case in 2023.The ruling leaves Thorpe with one domestic option: seeking permission to appeal to the High Court of Australia. The High Court accepts about 10% of applications for leave to appeal.Thorpe, an elder of the Krauatungalung people, said he did not expect a fair hearing in Australia and would take his allegations to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Netherlands after exhausting his domestic legal options.“The International Criminal Court will expose Australia for what it really is — a lying, racist, illegal occupation committing genocide,” Thorpe said.His case alleges that Charles, who is Australia's head of state, along with the Australian government and its institutions, is perpetuating genocide by maintaining systems that disadvantage Indigenous Australians across several socioeconomic measures.Indigenous Australians make up about 4% of the population and, according to official statistics, have shorter life expectancies, poorer health outcomes and higher rates of imprisonment and unemployment than other Australians.The monarch's legal immunity presents another hurdle. Sydney University constitutional lawyer Anne Twomey said the British monarch is protected from criminal and civil liability in the UK, including for personal acts outside official duties.She said the monarch's common law immunity has likely carried over to Australia, although she was unaware of it having been tested in an Australian court.The king is also protected by sovereign immunity under customary international law and Australian laws including the Foreign States Immunities Act 1985 and Diplomatic Privileges and Immunities Act 1967.The ICC does not recognise head-of-state immunity and can prosecute cases of genocide. However, individuals cannot directly launch private prosecutions there.Australian National University international lawyer Don Rothwell said individuals can instead submit evidence to the ICC prosecutor, as has happened in cases involving Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.“An individual cannot commence a prosecution,” Rothwell said. “It's then up to the International Criminal Court to determine whether they would seek to prosecute.”A UN Security Council referral is another possible route, but Rothwell said Britain would veto such a move against Charles.Thorpe has said he will pursue his allegations internationally after exhausting his options in Australia.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1901, Germany opened a “flying train” above the Wupper valley; 125 years later, it carries over 80,000 passengers daily
articles.summary: The Wuppertal Suspension Railway, which opened on 1 March 1901, has glided above the Wupper River for 125 years and now carries over 80,000 passengers
articles.body: The Wuppertal Suspension Railway, which opened on 1 March 1901, has glided above the Wupper River for 125 years and now carries over 80,000 passengers every day, according to Mayor Miriam Scherff. She says its suspended technology offers a fast, environmentally friendly link between districts along a 13-kilometre stretch of narrow valley, where a connection would otherwise be virtually impossible to manage. To mark the anniversary, Wuppertal's public utilities company, WSW, is running an orange and blue GTW 72 car, restoring the historic Kaiserwagen and planning a public festival in late summer 2026 that will focus on residents' personal stories.Why Germany built the “flying train” above the Wupper valleyScherff explains that the railway's technology, which suspends the cars above the Wupper, reduces traffic congestion and emissions in the city. According to the WSW official press release, it is a fast, environmentally friendly link between Wuppertal's districts. In her words, such a link would otherwise be virtually impossible to manage along a 13-kilometre stretch in the narrow valley.The Mayor also places the railway in the context of the city's history. She says it reflects the pioneering spirit and courage of the city leaders of the time, who dared to undertake ambitious urban development projects and take different paths. She calls it "the soul of our city" and describes it as unique worldwide. She also recounts riding it with her daughter for the first time, boarding at Oberbarmen to get a seat by the panoramic window. The two now ride regularly, sometimes with no particular destination.How Wuppertal is celebrating 125 years of its “flying train”WSW says the anniversary programme began on 8 January, when a car in the livery of the 1972 series (GTW 72) ran through the valley for the first time in many years. One of the current cars has been decorated in orange and blue in the GTW 72 design, and it will stay in regular service throughout the year. WSW is also collecting personal stories about the railway through a submission form on its website. These stories will be the focus of a public festival planned for late summer 2026, to which all Wuppertal residents are invited.The anniversary will also be visible across the city. WSW states that buses, service vehicles, posters and flags will carry the anniversary motto. A new 1:87 scale model of the GTW 72 car is available at WSW customer centres and in the Wuppertal Marketing online shop, and further merchandise, such as buttons and T-shirts, will follow during the year. The historic Kaiserwagen (Emperor's Car) is being restored for the anniversary, and WSW aims to have it back in service by May.How Germany’s “flying train” is being honoured with a special stampDeutsche Post is marking the anniversary with a special stamp in its "Time Travel Germany" series, according to the release. The stamp shows a photograph of Robert-Daum-Platz station, presented as it appeared in 1901 and as it appears today. A collectable first-day cover is also available, and both items were unveiled on 8 January.Sabine Schnake, Managing Director of WSW mobil, says the railway remains a "symbol of progress and courage" after 125 years. She adds that WSW is investing in technology and infrastructure to keep it fit for the coming decades, as a sustainable mobility solution for Wuppertal. WSW describes the wider WSW Group as covering energy supply, drinking water, public transport, urban drainage, energy services and waste management. It employs approximately 3,500 people and is one of Wuppertal's largest employers.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: From containment to commerce? Trump is said to make arms sales pitch to Xi
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: MAGA supremo Donald Trump has spent much of his presidency telling allies and partners, including India, to buy more
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: MAGA supremo Donald Trump has spent much of his presidency telling allies and partners, including India, to buy more American weapons. At his meeting with Xi Jinping, America’s top arms salesman apparently decided to extend the same customer-service offer to Washington’s principal military rival, China.In a jaw-dropping disclosure, a fall-out from which American mandarins are scrambling to contain, US ambassador to China David Perdue has revealed that President Trump offered to sell arms to China, since Washington sold weapons to many other countries around the world. “He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point,” the ambassador told Fox News Sunday amid a clattering of jaws to the floor across much of the world which sees China as a US adversary, and is looking to Washington’s leadership to meet challenges from Beijing.The State Department promptly applied diplomatic varnish to the bombshell, asserting that “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.” The White House likewise said there were no plans for such a sale, but the clanger rippled across the diplomatic world despite Trump’s reputation as a maverick who adopts unorthodox ways and means to diplomacy.Perdue himself reeled back from the implication that Trump is ready to throw Taiwan under the Chinese bus. “President Trump has already sold 50 percent more arms to Taiwan than any other president since 1979, and so I don't accept the premise that he's not doing all that we should be doing for Taiwan,” he said in a follow-up post on X. Four Republican senators last week separately urged the administration to uphold US defense commitments to Taiwan.Countries from Japan to Australia to India would be affected by any policy pivot that results in arms sales to China, but the stakes are particularly high in Taiwan. Xi's Washington visit came as Beijing was pressing Trump to halt arms sales to the island, while Taiwan awaits a roughly $14 billion US package that Trump has previously described as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China. But the episode has inevitably raised questions in Taipei and among Washington's China hawks about whether Taiwan's security can become a bargaining chip in a Trump-Xi transaction.For US allies and partners, who have been building their defense strategies around the assumption that Washington regards China's military power as a rival and a threat, Trump’s suggestion that Beijing might be a customer for American weaponry would create an extraordinary strategic contradiction, notwithstanding the legal obstacle his administration would face in funneling arms to China. The US has maintained restrictions on arms exports to China since the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown. Current federal regulations place China under a policy of denial for defense articles and services, while the statutory framework suspends licensing for exports of US Munitions List defense articles, subject to narrow exceptions.The last substantial US military sales to China date to the 1980s, before Tiananmen, and they included 24 Sikorsky S-70C helicopters, F-8 fighter avionics modernization, artillery-locating radars, Mark 46 anti-submarine torpedoes and assistance for artillery-ammunition production. Washington suspended the military relationship after the June 1989 crackdown, but previously authorized equipment was subsequently delivered under limited exceptions.Perdue himself is far from a China hawk. Before politics and diplomacy, he was a corporate executive steeped in manufacturing in and sourcing from Asia. He worked in Singapore and Hong Kong and ran Asian operations for Sara Lee, sourcing from China and Hong Kong, before senior roles at Haggar and Reebok, which sourced all its production from Asia. Some critics have noted that the man now charged with managing Washington's most consequential strategic rivalry was once getting US companies to make things in Asia as cheaply and efficiently as possible.The larger question though is whether the episode represents merely Trump's characteristic negotiating theater or something more consequential. His foreign policy has repeatedly emphasized deals, leverage, money and personal relationships. Many experts have warned that treating alliances and strategic commitments as negotiable assets risks making long-standing friends wonder whether their security ultimately has a price.Such concern is especially relevant for India, according to officials who spoke on background. If arms to China can be floated as a commercial proposition, however casually, America's willingness to supply weapons to other countries -- including Pakistan, should Washington's currently warming relationship with Islamabad deepen -- could increasingly be viewed through a transactional rather than strategic lens.Trump's attraction to strongmen such as Xi Jinping and Kim Un-Sung has likewise unsettled traditional foreign-policy assumptions. The administration argues that personal diplomacy can produce deals that conventional statecraft cannot, but even former US analysts see a different pattern: democratic partners being rudely slapped with tariffs and sanctions, while authoritarian regimes receive red carpet welcomes.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Ohio lawyer accidentally sent $550 to a stranger on Zelle; the payment mistake turned into a three-year court battle
articles.summary: Christine Baker, an Ohio lawyer, attempted to make payments to her husband via Zelle, worth $550, in September 2023.
articles.body: Christine Baker, an Ohio lawyer, attempted to make payments to her husband via Zelle, worth $550, in September 2023. She ended up making two payments to Zachary W. Reynolds, who was from Illinois and a total stranger to her. An error that she noticed the very next day, and hence made contact with Reynolds to seek the return of the payment. Reynolds was cautious about returning the amount to a total stranger; thus, he told her that the matter should be sorted out through his bank, Charles Schwab. The money, therefore, was returned to him in October 2023. Nevertheless, this was not the end of the story; rather, it resulted in a lawsuit, which further escalated into an appeal in the Ohio courts in September 2026.How the Ohio lawyer accidentally sent $550 through ZelleThe mistake happened on September 19 and 20, 2023, when Baker sent two payments totalling $550 through Zelle. According to the Ohio Court of Appeals opinion, Baker had intended to send the payments to her husband’s bank account. Her husband shared the same first and last name as Reynolds, while their email addresses were very similar, which contributed to the mix-up. Baker discovered what had happened the day after the second payment. She then used the internet to find Reynolds and his contact information, as well as information for his wife and some of his co-workers.Reynolds did not immediately send the money backOn September 22, Baker contacted Reynolds through email, text message and LinkedIn. The court record says some of those communications threatened litigation if the $550 was not returned within 24 hours. Reynolds did not immediately transfer the money because his bank had advised him about the situation, and he was concerned that he could be the target of a financial scam. He instead suggested that Baker contact Charles Schwab to resolve the matter. Baker subsequently contacted Reynolds’s wife and several co-workers, and she also emailed the Kettering Police Department about the matter. Reynolds hired an Illinois attorney to communicate with her.The $550 was returned, but the dispute moved into courtThe payment was eventually returned to Baker on October 3, 2023, about two weeks after she had mistakenly sent it. Reynolds then filed a grievance against Baker with the Dayton Bar Association over what the court described as her aggressive tactics following the mistaken payment. Baker responded by filing a lawsuit against Reynolds alleging conversion and defamation claims. The case was removed to federal court, where Baker voluntarily dismissed it without prejudice in January 2024. After the Dayton Bar Association notified Baker in September 2024 of its intent to file a formal disciplinary complaint, she refiled her civil case in Montgomery County Common Pleas Court in October 2024.The case reached the Ohio Court of Appeals in 2026Reynolds moved for summary judgment in July 2025 on the grounds that Baker’s allegations did not hold up legally. This motion was granted by the trial court on February 27, 2026. Baker filed an appeal challenging the trial court’s ruling and contending that there were unresolved issues of fact and that the trial court misapplied privilege and other rules. The Second District Court of Appeals upheld the trial court’s decision on September 4, 2026. It emphasised that Baker did not put forth any evidence that challenged Reynolds’ motion for summary judgment or that showed any factual dispute existed on the record. From Baker sending a mistaken payment of $550 via Zelle in September 2023, this legal issue had turned into a three-year-old case.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Seattle shipbuilder sold his company for a reported $3.5 million in 1906 and built an Orcas Island estate; 15 years later he donated more than 2,700 acres to Washington to create Moran State Park
articles.summary: In 1905, doctors told Seattle shipbuilder and former mayor Robert Moran that he had only six months to live because of severe exhaustion.
articles.body: In 1905, doctors told Seattle shipbuilder and former mayor Robert Moran that he had only six months to live because of severe exhaustion. The next year, he sold his shipbuilding company for a reported $3.5 million, moved to Orcas Island, and lived for another 37 years. That major change not only gave Moran a quieter life but also changed the landscape of Washington state. Fifteen years after moving to the San Juan Islands, Moran gave more than 2,700 acres of his private estate to the state government. The gift became what is now Moran State Park. Historical records from HistoryLink, the online encyclopedia of Washington state history, and the Washington State Parks Field Guide blog document Moran's role in creating the park.Rise of a Seattle industrialistBorn in New York City in 1857, Robert Moran arrived in Seattle in 1875 with just 10 cents in his pocket. He found work as a ship's engineer before starting a marine repair shop with his brothers along the Seattle waterfront. That small workshop grew into Moran Brothers Company, which became one of the largest shipbuilding yards in the Pacific Northwest. The company gained national attention after winning a federal contract to build the USS Nebraska, a Virginia-class battleship for the United States Navy. HistoryLink identifies the Nebraska as the only battleship built in Washington state. HistoryLink records that Moran also served two terms as mayor of Seattle. He took office after the Great Seattle Fire of 1889 and helped rebuild the city's central business district and modernize its public water system. The pressure of running a major shipyard and overseeing work on the battleship damaged Moran's health. In 1905, his doctors told him he had organic heart disease and might have no more than six months to live. Moran later described his condition as the result of a highly nervous state caused by an overworked physical and mental life.Building Rosario on Orcas IslandMoran followed the doctors' warning. In 1906, he sold Moran Brothers Company to the New York firm Berton-Griscom and Company for a reported $3.5 million. He used his wealth to acquire thousands of acres on Orcas Island, the largest island in the San Juan archipelago. Between 1906 and 1909, Moran built Rosario, a 54-room mansion overlooking Cascade Bay. HistoryLink describes Rosario as a maritime-inspired Arts and Crafts mansion. According to the Washington State Parks Field Guide blog, Moran brought the same careful approach to his home that he had used in shipbuilding. Rosario included strong construction and systems designed for the remote island setting. The estate also had its own hydroelectric power system and water system. The property became the center of Moran's large private estate. He eventually acquired about 7,800 acres that included forests, lakes, shoreline and Mount Constitution, the highest point in the San Juan Islands.Gift of land to Washington stateWhile living at Rosario, Moran acquired a large amount of wilderness land around Mount Constitution. By 1921, Moran had decided that the forests, lakes and mountain areas around his home should be protected rather than developed. He formally gave 2,731 acres to the State of Washington for use as a public park. The state accepted the donation in April 1921, and Moran State Park was established. Moran had first tried to give land to the state several years earlier. HistoryLink reports that he offered 3,000 acres in 1911, but the state did not yet have the organization or funding needed to manage such a large park. After Moran removed the conditions on his offer and reduced the proposed donation to 2,731 acres, the state finally accepted it in 1921. During the Great Depression in the 1930s, the Civilian Conservation Corps built major facilities in the park. Its work included trails, roads, bridges, stone shelters and the landmark 53-foot stone observation tower that still stands on Mount Constitution. The tower was completed in 1936.Legacy of conservation in the San JuansToday, Moran State Park covers more than 5,000 acres after expanding through additional land purchases and donations. HistoryLink describes it as one of Washington's most popular park destinations. The park includes five freshwater lakes, miles of forest trails and wide views across the San Juan Islands, Vancouver Island, the Olympic Peninsula, Mount Baker and the Cascade Range. The park's trail system covers about 38 miles. Moran lived at Rosario until 1938, when he sold the estate and moved to a smaller house on Orcas Island. He died in 1943 at age 86, nearly four decades after doctors had warned that he had only months to live. Rosario was later converted into a resort and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1977. Moran's hydroelectric plant still supplies the property with power. Much of the land he gave to Washington remains protected as Moran State Park and is open for public recreation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Texas oil geologist first saw McKittrick Canyon in 1921, later bought the land for a private retreat; 38 years later he donated 4,942 acres and his home, helping create Guadalupe Mountains National Park
articles.summary: When petroleum geologist Wallace Pratt first visited McKittrick Canyon in 1921, he had been sent to West Texas on a trip with oil brokers to acquire
articles.body: When petroleum geologist Wallace Pratt first visited McKittrick Canyon in 1921, he had been sent to West Texas on a trip with oil brokers to acquire leases for Humble Oil and Refining Company. Local land brokers offered to show him what they called the most beautiful spot in Texas, a hidden oasis of clear streams, waterfalls and lush greenery in the Chihuahuan Desert. Impressed by the canyon's geology and natural beauty, Pratt bought land there with two business partners to use as a private summer retreat. Nearly four decades later, that personal refuge became the foundation for Guadalupe Mountains National Park. According to historical records maintained by the National Park Service, Pratt's first land donation included 4,942 acres and was accepted by the federal government in 1959. He and his family later gave an additional 690 acres between 1960 and 1961. Together, these gifts formed the core of the land that became Guadalupe Mountains National Park in 1972.Building a stone sanctuary in the canyonPratt's first development in McKittrick Canyon was simple and practical. During the winter of 1931 and 1932, he hired architect John Staubs to build Pratt Cabin, a two-bedroom stone structure made with locally quarried stone and timber. The Pratt family used the cabin as a summer home. But its location deep inside the canyon, near a wash, left it exposed to strong floods and bad weather. The family continued using it as a retreat even after building a second home on higher ground. After Pratt's first wife, Pearl, died in 1940, he married Iris Calderhead in 1941. Calderhead was a prominent early 20th-century suffragist and former leader of the National Woman's Party. Soon after their marriage, the couple decided to build a permanent home on higher ground near the mouth of McKittrick Canyon.Architectural marvel inspired by oil tankersTo design their new home, the Pratts hired the New York City architecture firm Milliken and Bevin. The house, completed in 1943 and named Ship on the Desert, became an important early example of modernist architecture in West Texas. According to National Park Service records, the house was designed to look like an ocean-going oil tanker. The design reflected Pratt's long career in the oil industry. The long, narrow home used local limestone, wide areas of glass and a layout designed to blend with the surrounding mountains. The design also included details tied to Iris Pratt's life. The entrance door was painted bright purple, a color linked to the women's suffrage movement and the National Woman's Party. Although Milliken and Bevin received formal credit for the design, Pratt's letters credited Newton and Elizabeth Bevin with much of the actual design work. The couple stayed at the original Pratt Cabin while supervising construction of the new house. National Park Service records say construction began in 1942 and was completed in 1943.Conservation gift and creation of a national parkWallace and Iris Pratt lived at Ship on the Desert for about 15 years. Wallace kept an office in Carlsbad, New Mexico, and often flew his small plane from the private airstrip near the house to his office. The Pratts also operated a ranch from the property. As Iris's health declined, the couple moved to Tucson, Arizona, around 1960. Pratt wanted to protect McKittrick Canyon and the Guadalupe Mountains from future development. Beginning in 1959, he began giving his land to the federal government. The first donation, accepted on December 30, 1959, covered 4,942 acres. A second donation involving 690 acres was accepted in 1960 and 1961. The National Park Service says the total Pratt property accepted by the government was 5,632 acres. Pratt's gift helped drive the effort to create a national park. The federal government later purchased about 80,000 acres owned by rancher and developer J.C. Hunter Jr. to complete the larger park area. Congress passed the legislation needed to establish Guadalupe Mountains National Park in 1966. The land transfer was completed by 1970, and the park was formally dedicated and opened to the public in September 1972. The park now covers 76,293 acres and includes Guadalupe Peak, the highest point in Texas, as well as the extensive exposed Permian fossil reef for which the Guadalupe Mountains are known.Preservation status of the Pratt structuresBoth of Pratt's historic residences remain preserved inside Guadalupe Mountains National Park today. Pratt Cabin is located along the McKittrick Canyon Trail and is a popular stop for hikers. The cabin is now an interpretive site that tells the story of the Pratt family. The building is not normally open to the public unless a volunteer or ranger is present. Ship on the Desert was added to the National Register of Historic Places and remains under National Park Service care. Over the years, it has been used as housing for staff and volunteers and as a research center for scientists studying the park's geology. It is not currently open to the public. In 2018, the National Trust for Historic Preservation placed Ship on the Desert on its list of America's 11 Most Endangered Historic Places. The National Trust cited deferred maintenance and the need for preservation work on the early modernist building. The National Park Service continues efforts to raise funds and plan restoration work to protect the house for future study.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Omar Abdullah: If guns decide statehood, Pakistan will decide
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: CM Omar Abdullah said Monday that making J&K statehood conditional on the end of militancy would effectively give Pakistan a say in its
articles.body: SRINAGAR: CM Omar Abdullah said Monday that making J&K statehood conditional on the end of militancy would effectively give Pakistan a say in its restoration, as the assembly passed a resolution for full statehood and set off a BJP walkout over its reference to a 2000 autonomy demand.Omar moved the resolution that calls on Union govt to restore full statehood. It refers to the 2000 assembly resolution accepting the state autonomy committee report and seeking greater autonomy, and a 2024 resolution seeking special status and constitutional guarantees for J&K.National Conference, Congress, PDP, Peoples Conference, Awami Ithaad Party and CPM supported it.BJP’s Sunil Sharma called the resolution “anti-constitutional” and “anti-secular”, saying its reference to the 2000 autonomy resolution amounted to seeking restoration of J&K’s “pre-1953 position”. BJP said it supports restoration of statehood but opposes the resolution in its current form. Its legislators entered the well, shouted “Vande Mataram” and “Bharat Mata Ki Jai” and moved a motion against speaker Abdul Rahim Rather.Omar criticised BJP’s opinion that statehood could be restored only after militancy ends. “Then the decision regarding restoration of the statehood will not be taken directly in New Delhi but it will be taken in Islamabad,” he said, adding if Pakistan is blamed for militancy, making restoration conditional on guns falling silent effectively gives Islamabad a say in when J&K gets statehood.“We are not begging,” Omar said. “We rightfully demand that we have the right to a statehood.”Omar said the resolution was rooted in a promise of restoring statehood and had nothing to do with Article 370, 35A or autonomy. J&K lost statehood and was bifurcated into two Union territories, including Ladakh, in Aug 2019 when Centre also scrapped its special constitutional status.The CM said he had deliberately kept Article 370, 35A and special status out of the resolution to prevent BJP from using them to disrupt proceedings. He also criticised NC members who had moved amendments seeking references to Article 370 and 35A, saying they had provided BJP “an excuse to oppose it”.Omar said Supreme Court had directed Centre to restore statehood “at the earliest” after assembly elections in 2024 and questioned whether two years could qualify as “as soon as possible”. Omar said there was still no clarity on when Centre considered the “right time” for restoration.Deputy CM Surinder Choudhary rejected BJP’s position that J&K’s sensitive location justified its UT status, saying nearly half of India’s states share borders with neighbouring countries.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: At 17, British student Alex Chui scores a perfect 42/42 at the Maths Olympiad, winning his fifth gold medal in seven appearances
articles.summary: A perfect score is unusual at the International Mathematical Olympiad, where contestants face six demanding problems over two four-and-a-half-hour papers.
articles.body: A perfect score is unusual at the International Mathematical Olympiad, where contestants face six demanding problems over two four-and-a-half-hour papers. According to UK Olympiads, in 2026, just seven of the 666 competitors managed to collect all 42 points. One of them was Britain’s Alex Chui, a 17-year-old from Tonbridge School.His result in Shanghai was also the latest entry in an unusual international record. Chui had already won gold medals at four previous editions of the competition. The 2026 gold made it five, while his appearances across seven editions produced seven medals in total. Britain finished ninth among 117 participating teams, with six medals shared between its six competitors.Alex Chui turns a perfect 42 into seven medals from seven IMO appearancesChui’s 42 points came from six full-mark problems. He received 7 points on each question, leaving no partial score or missed mark on his final paper.The result placed him joint first individually. Only seven students reached the maximum score across the entire competition, which brought together 666 contestants representing 117 teams.Reportedly, for Chui, however, the perfect paper was part of a much longer record. He had already collected IMO gold medals in 2021, 2023, 2024 and 2025. His fifth gold in Shanghai completed a run in which every one of his seven appearances produced a medal. That gives him seven medals from seven participations, including five golds.Britain returns from Shanghai with six medalsThe British team finished with two golds, one silver and three bronze medals. Kevin Wai of Magdalen College School joined Chui in the gold-medal group after scoring 29 points. Yuvan Raja of RGS Guildford took silver with 26 points. Adavya Goyal of St Paul's School, along with Anango Prabhat and Michael Sydorenko of King's Maths School, each scored 22 and received bronze.The six students therefore all returned with medals. Their combined score was 163 points. That total placed Britain ninth in the team standings. North Korea also scored 163 points, but the two teams were separated by their medal distribution. North Korea had two golds and two silvers alongside two bronzes, while Britain had two golds, one silver and three bronzes.Six problems, 42 points and a 29-point gold medal cut-off in ShanghaiThe International Mathematical Olympiad is built around six problems, divided between two examination days. Contestants have 4.5 hours on each day to tackle three questions. Each problem carries a maximum of seven points, giving a possible total of 42. The questions are designed around areas such as geometry, number theory, algebra and combinatorics, rather than the routine calculations associated with school mathematics.At the 2026 event in Shanghai, the results stretched from perfect scores at the top to a large number of contestants receiving no medal. There were 55 gold medals, 105 silvers and 189 bronzes, while 141 competitors received honourable mentions, as reported by The UK Olympiads and IMO2026.The gold threshold was 29 points. Wai's score landed exactly on that boundary.Seven medals across seven appearancesChui's longer record is perhaps the most distinctive part of the 2026 result. His five IMO gold medals came in 2021, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026. The two remaining appearances also ended with medals, giving him seven medals from seven editions.The perfect 42 in Shanghai added another distinction to that record. Of the seven contestants who achieved a maximum score in 2026, Chui was the British representative, alongside three competitors from China, two from the United States and one from South Korea.At 17, his competition career at the IMO has now produced an unusually complete sequence: seven appearances, seven medals and five golds, capped by a 42-point performance in his latest contest.You use AI every day. articles.title: Father left $21 million in a charitable fund; son sought a $1 million donation but his access was cut off by the foundation
articles.summary: A $21 million charitable fund is at the centre of a legal dispute after Philip Peterson, the son of its founder, alleged that WaterStone cut off his
articles.body: A $21 million charitable fund is at the centre of a legal dispute after Philip Peterson, the son of its founder, alleged that WaterStone cut off his access and stopped acting on his recommendations. The fund was created by Gordon Peterson in 2005 for Christian charitable causes, and Philip became its sole successor adviser after his mother died. According to the lawsuit, the dispute escalated in 2024, when access to the account was revoked and a proposed $1 million donation was not processed. The case is now examining how much authority successor advisers actually have over donor-advised funds.How did the $21 million fund become the subject of a lawsuitGordon Peterson established the Peterson Family Stewardship Fund with WaterStone in 2005. The fund was intended to support evangelical Christian charitable purposes. WaterStone, the name used by Christian Community Foundation, became responsible for holding and administering the money.According to MinistryWatch, Gordon died in 2019. His wife Ruth and son Philip had been recognised as advisers to the family fund from 2017. When Ruth died in 2021, Philip became the sole successor adviser. For several years, WaterStone continued to process the charitable grants he recommended.The fund was worth more than $21 million by the end of 2023, according to the lawsuit. CNBC reported that Peterson had continued to make recommendations from the account until the relationship with WaterStone deteriorated in 2024. At that point, he says, his access to information about the fund was cut off.What changed between Peterson and WaterStoneThe disagreement appears to have centred on how the fund would be managed and distributed in the future. CNBC reported that Peterson disagreed with WaterStone over a proposal concerning the fund's principal and investment income. He subsequently raised the possibility of moving the fund to another sponsor.According to MinistryWatch, Peterson says a March 5, 2024 Zoom call with WaterStone chief executive Ken Harrison ended with Peterson being told that further communication with the organisation would cease. Peterson then tried to restore access and contacted board members, but says those efforts did not resolve the dispute.The lawsuit alleges that WaterStone revoked his online access, suspended his advisory privileges and stopped processing his grant recommendations. Foley & Lardner reported that Peterson also alleges WaterStone refused to provide information about the account and directed him to stop contacting the organisation.$1 million donation at the centre of the disputeOne of the most significant recommendations involved a proposed $1 million grant to Operation Mobilization, a Christian missionary organisation that had previously received support from the Peterson family fund.MinistryWatch reported that Peterson says WaterStone denied the distribution after previously approving and administering his recommendations. It also reported that the fund made no charitable grants in 2024, according to the lawsuit.The issue was particularly important to Peterson because Operation Mobilization had a history of receiving support from his family. His lawsuit argues that WaterStone's actions interfered with the charitable purpose for which his father had established the fund.In February 2025, WaterStone agreed to make $400,000 in distributions, according to MinistryWatch. Peterson accepted those distributions but also raised concerns that the fund was still behind on charitable contributions from earlier years.What does the lawsuit say about control of donor-advised fundsThe case raises a broader issue because a donor-advised fund does not work like a personal bank account for charitable giving. Once money is contributed, the sponsoring organisation legally controls the assets, while the donor or successor adviser can recommend where grants should go.Foley & Lardner explained that this distinction is central to this case. The law firm said WaterStone's sponsorship agreement gives it ultimate control and discretion over the fund and states that the original donor irrevocably gave up ownership and other rights to the contributions. That arrangement is common to donor-advised funds. The adviser can have an important role in suggesting charitable grants, but the sponsor retains legal control over the money.The case could clarify duties and rights of successor advisers and sponsorsPeterson's lawsuit seeks more than the payment of one disputed grant. According to MinistryWatch, he is asking for an accounting of the fund, clarification of the rights and duties between himself and WaterStone, and an order requiring the organisation to carry out its responsibilities, including recommended grants. He is also seeking to transfer the fund to another organisation.Foley & Lardner reports that the case could clarify whether advisory rights that donors and successor advisers commonly rely upon are legally enforceable. WaterStone has argued in its motion to dismiss that it is not contractually required to follow Peterson's recommendations because the sponsorship agreement leaves ultimate authority with WaterStone.The case reaches beyond the Peterson family. It could help clarify what happens when a donor-advised fund sponsor and a successor adviser no longer agree about how charitable money should be handled.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cracked pillar sparks panic, 25 families evacuated from SA apartment
articles.summary: Cracked pillar in Lucknow’s SA Apartment triggered evacuation of 25 families; LDA sealed building and probed alleged extra floors, construction violations.
articles.body: Lucknow: Panic gripped residents of SA Apartment in Wazirganj area on Monday morning after a pillar in the five-storey building developed cracks, prompting authorities to evacuate all 25 families living there as a precautionary measure.The incident was reported around 10:30 am when several residents said they felt a sudden jolt and noticed structural movement inside the building. Many initially mistook the vibration for an earthquake, but soon discovered that a pillar had cracked. Although the structure remained standing, the visible damage triggered alarm and residents rushed outside.Police, along with teams from State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), reached the site and carried out an evacuation. The area around the apartment was barricaded and movement in the vicinity was restricted to prevent any mishap while officials assessed the risk.Mohammed Israr, a resident, said his wife narrowly escaped injury when the pillar cracked as she was standing on a balcony. He alleged that residents had been flagging concerns about the building’s condition for the past six to seven months but no effective action was taken by those responsible for maintenance. “I bought this flat for around Rs 17 lakh. My entire savings are invested in it,” he said.Lucknow Development Authority (LDA) officials said the damaged pillar was located on the ground floor of SA Apartment built on plot number 179/30C in the Baroodkhana locality of Wazirganj.LDA secretary Sushil Pratap Singh, additional secretary Gyanendra Verma and zonal officer Prabhakar Singh visited the site and supervised operations with the district administration and police.Preliminary records reviewed by LDA indicate that landowner Shahabuddin applied for a building plan on May 25, 2009, and the map was sanctioned on Aug 12, 2009, under permit number 26520. After the evacuation, LDA’s Enforcement Zone-6 sealed the building as a safety measure while rescue and safety work continued.During an inspection, officials also began examining records related to construction and structural stability. Initial scrutiny raised questions over whether floors had been added beyond what was originally approved. “The map was initially sanctioned for a three-storey building in the name of Shahabuddin. We are now being told by the owner that two additional floors were constructed after compounding, but no supporting records have been produced so far,” said Prabhakar Singh.District magistrate Vishak G said the building was evacuated immediately after information was received and that teams were continuously monitoring the structure. He added that accommodation would be arranged at a night shelter for residents who had nowhere else to stay.Mayor Sushma Kharkwal, who visited the spot, said the incident raised serious questions about construction quality and possible violations.Three years after Alaya disaster, another building raises alarmMore than three years after the collapse of Alaya Apartment on Wazir Hasan Road, structural concerns have surfaced at SA Apartment in Lucknow. The 2023 Alaya tragedy claimed three lives and injured 14 people. articles.title: Ayushman shield saves over 108 hearts and lives everyday
articles.summary: Ayushman Bharat (PMJAY) has helped save 108 cardiac patients daily in UP since 2018, funding Rs 2,116.7 crore for advanced procedures, officials say.
articles.body: Lucknow: Some 108 hearts and lives at risk of cardiac complications have been saved every single day over the past eight years with the help of Ayushman Bharat, an assessment of official data sourced on the eve of World Heart Day showed.This translates into a benefit extended to an average of 39,430 persons per year and totals 3,15,444 lives since the launch of the scheme in 2018.“For many poor families in UP, cardiac emergency meant a catastrophic financial ruin pushing families into the pit of medical poverty with little or no hope of recovery as those affected were usually the breadwinners,” said CEO of State Agency for Comprehensive Health and Integrated Services (SACHIS), Archana Verma.She said UP sanctioned over Rs 2,116.70 crore for advanced cardiac procedures.Citing numbers, Verma said over 1% of the beneficiaries were children afflicted with congenital heart diseases and defects while every third life saved was that of a woman who was earlier left to fate. “Before Ayushman scheme, many children and women died untreated as per social impact studies. A large number of these patients were from rural and peri-urban areas,” she said.President-elect of Cardiological Society of India, Satyendra Tewari, said: “India now loses more people to cardiovascular disease—heart attack, stroke, heart failure and related conditions—than any other cause. It is responsible for every fourth death which totals to 24 to 25 lakh lives annually.”Tewari noted that the average age of a first heart attack in India is 53 to 57 years—at least a decade earlier than in Western nations.He warned of a dual burden: persistent legacy conditions like rheumatic heart disease alongside surging ischaemic heart disease driven by sedentary habits, stress and specific genetic risks.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: In 1930, former Maine governor Percival Baxter bought nearly 6,000 acres around Mount Katahdin; 32 years later, his final acquisition brought his gifted parkland to 201,018 acres, now part of a 209,644-acre park
articles.summary: A former governor of Maine built one of North America’s largest state parks piece by piece over three decades.
articles.body: A former governor of Maine built one of North America’s largest state parks piece by piece over three decades. He paid for every purchase with his own money after efforts to use public funds failed. Percival P. Baxter made his first purchase, 5,960 acres around Mount Katahdin, in 1930. By the time he made his final land gift 32 years later, he had given 201,018 acres to the people of Maine. Later land purchases, gifts, and transfers increased the total size of Baxter State Park to 209,644 acres, according to records from the Baxter State Park Authority. The land campaign remains one of the largest efforts by one person to protect land in American history.A political defeat turns into a private campaignBaxter first tried to protect Mount Katahdin while serving in the Maine State Legislature during the 1920s. He introduced bills to create a state park around Maine’s highest peak, but his efforts failed. Timber interests and political opposition stood in the way. When Baxter left public office in 1925, he stopped trying to create the park through politics and decided to buy the wilderness himself. He spent the next 32 years dealing directly with private timber firms, paper companies, and individual landowners across northern Maine. “Man is born to die, his works are short-lived,” Baxter wrote in a letter to the Maine Legislature with his first deed of gift in 1931. “Buildings crumble, monuments decay, wealth vanishes, but Katahdin in all its glory forever shall remain the mountain of the people of Maine.” His method was unusual for conservation projects at the time. Instead of using eminent domain or state money, Baxter bought the land with his family fortune. His father had built that fortune through a canned goods business and real estate investments.Binding trust deeds protect the wildernessTo make sure the land stayed wild, Baxter put strict conditions into his 28 separate deeds of trust given to the state between 1931 and 1962. The Baxter State Park Authority’s records say Baxter required most of the park to “forever be kept in the natural wild state” and remain a sanctuary for wild animals and birds. His deeds banned industrial development, paving, and some forms of commercial recreation. He also kept the park outside Maine’s regular state park system. The goal was to prevent future state governments from changing the rules Baxter had set. “State Park rules do not apply to Baxter State Park,” says the management plan published by the Baxter State Park Authority. Instead, the park is run by a three-member authority made up of the Maine attorney general, the director of the Maine Forest Service, and the commissioner of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife. Baxter also created trust funds to help pay for park operations without depending on Maine taxpayer money or regular state appropriations.Managed forestry vs absolute wildernessBaxter wanted the central mountain area to stay wild, but he gave different instructions for the northern part of the park. From 1955 to 1962, Baxter acquired more than 28,000 acres in the northern section and set it aside as the Scientific Forest Management Area. His deeds said this land should be managed with sustainable forestry methods. The goal was to show how timber production and forest protection could work together. The park now identifies the area as 29,537 acres. The park’s management documents say timber is selectively harvested in this area. Revenue from the harvest helps support park operations. The park’s 2025 forest management plan also includes projected timber revenue as part of the area’s financial planning.Expanding the footprint beyond 200,000 acresBaxter made his final land gift in 1962, at age 86, bringing his direct gifts to 201,018 acres. He died seven years later, in 1969. After his death, the park continued to grow through land trades, purchases, and transfers. Later additions, including land near Trout Mountain and other boundary changes, brought the park’s total area to 209,644 acres. Today, the park contains more than 40 mountain peaks and ridges, including Mount Katahdin’s Baxter Peak. The peak rises to about 5,268 feet and marks the northern end of the roughly 2,200-mile Appalachian Trail. Park rules limit vehicle traffic and campsite sizes. Campgrounds also do not have electricity or running water. These limits help preserve the wilderness setting Baxter established through his original deeds.You use AI every day. articles.title: 14 dead in massive blaze at Russian fireworks factory
articles.summary: At least 14 people were killed in a fire at a fireworks factory in Russia’s Yaroslavl region on Monday, Russian state media reported, citing emergency
articles.body: At least 14 people were killed in a fire at a fireworks factory in Russia’s Yaroslavl region on Monday, Russian state media reported, citing emergency services. One person was injured in the blaze, according to state news agency TASS, which cited Russia’s emergency ministry.“The death toll from a fire at a fireworks factory in the Yaroslavl region has risen to 14, with one person injured,” TASS reported, citing the emergency ministry.The fire broke out at a pyrotechnics factory in the village of Kubrinsk, about 100 kilometres (62 miles) north of Moscow, according to TASS. The blaze engulfed two buildings at the site.Around 100 emergency personnel were deployed to contain the fire, Yaroslavl region governor Mikhail Evrayev said.Video published by state-owned broadcaster RT appeared to show bright sparks shooting from a smouldering pile of rubble following the blaze.The cause of the fire was not immediately established. Russian authorities have opened a criminal case over alleged violations of industrial safety regulations, state media reported.The region’s prosecution service said it had also opened an investigation into possible violations of industrial safety rules. However, officials had not yet publicly established whether safety violations caused Monday’s fire.Emergency services continued operations at the site as authorities assessed the damage and worked to establish the circumstances surrounding the deaths and injury.You use AI every day.
